raw_case_text:
A 2-month-old male infant was admitted to our hospital with a 1 month history of persistent white stools.
The meconium of the child was dark green. Three days later, his stool turned yellow. After that, the stool color gradually became white stool over the next month. The test results of the infant's liver function were: albumin 16.5 g/L, total bilirubin (TB) 35.2 mumol/l, direct bilirubin (DB) 27.7 mumol/l, and total bile acid (TBA) 63.0 mumol/l. The child had taken probiotics and the symptoms did not improve.
The patient had no significant past medical history. And the mother's pregnancy was uneventful.
At the time of admission, the infant's body weight was 3400 g (<3rd percentile) and his height was 60 cm (50-70th percentile). The physical examination revealed hepatomegaly (4 cm below the ribs with soft texture) and pitting edema of both lower limbs. No abnormality was revealed for the consciousness, cardiopulmonary examination, and nervous system examination.
Routine laboratory testing upon admission showed hemoglobin was 63 g/L, packed cell volume 19.9%, normal mean-cell volume, mean cell hemoglobin concentration was at the lower end of normal, and platelets 304 x 109/L. The patient was tested negative for hepatitis A, B, and, C, syphilis, HIV, TORCH, EBV-IgM antibody, and EBV DNA; his thyroid function and blood coagulation function were within the normal range. The patient's blood glucose during admission was normal and blood and urine tandem mass spectrometry showed that the amino acid and acylcarnitine spectrum analysis were normal. Cytomegalovirus IgM test was positive. Liver function tests revealed slightly elevated levels of TB, DB, and gamma-glutamyltransferase (gamma-GT) (shown in Table 1).
The cardiac ultrasound showed no abnormalities. The chest radiograph was normal. Abdominal ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly, liver parenchyma echoes, but the gallbladder and pancreas were normal.
In order to differentially diagnose whether there is biliary atresia (BA), we perfected the examination of liver, gallbladder, spleen color Doppler ultrasound, and gallbladder contraction. In order to differentially diagnose cardiogenic edema, we perfected the cardiac color Doppler ultrasound. The infant's parents refused to permit cholangiography and a liver biopsy. Due to the unclear diagnosis, we performed a genetic test. The infant's genetic analysis showed a CFTR hemizygous mutation site (c.223C>T) in exon 3 and exon 2-3 heterozygous deletion mutation. A genetic verification of the infant's parents was also performed; the father had a point mutation and the mother had a CFTR gene exon 2-3 heterozygous deletion mutation (shown in Figure 1). To further verify whether the child had pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, we tested fecal pancreas elastase 1 and the result was 0.6 mug/g, significantly lower than the normal value of 200 mug/g. Stool testing showed fat globules of 70-80/HP. These findings, combined with the manifestations of cholestasis, supported the diagnosis of CF. Because our hospitals and other testing institutions cannot perform a sweat chloride test, we did not perform it.
After hospital admission, the infant was placed on a lactose-free fortified medium-chain fatty acid milk powder feeding, oral ursodeoxycholic acid (UDCA) 30 mg/(kg.d), and supplemented with fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K. The stool color remained unchanged. Fecal pancreas elastase 1 suggested that the child had insufficient pancreatic exocrine function, so aspergillus oryzae pancreatic enzymes tablets (half a tablet once, three times per day) were added 2 weeks after diagnosis. Two weeks after the oral pancreatic enzyme tablets were administered, the color of the infant's stool changed to yellow and his weight increased (shown in Figure 2).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 2-month-old male infant presented with a 1-month history of persistent acholic (white) stools, failure to thrive, and bilateral lower-extremity edema.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Born after an uneventful pregnancy with normal dark-green meconium that turned yellow on day 3 of life, the infant developed progressively acholic white stools over the second month of life that did not improve with probiotics, accompanied by severe hypoalbuminemia, cholestasis, poor weight gain, and lower-limb pitting edema.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uneventful prenatal and birth history; no significant past medical history.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for 1 month of persistent white stools, poor weight gain (<3rd percentile), and bilateral lower-extremity edema.

objective.physical_examination: Body weight 3,400 g (<3rd percentile), length 60 cm (50-70th percentile); soft hepatomegaly palpable 4 cm below the costal margin and bilateral lower-extremity pitting edema; normal consciousness, cardiopulmonary, and neurological examinations.
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-admission LFTs: severe hypoalbuminemia (albumin 16.5 g/L), total bilirubin 35.2 umol/L, direct bilirubin 27.7 umol/L, and total bile acids 63.0 umol/L (admission LFTs also showed mildly elevated TB, DB, and GGT). Admission CBC: severe normocytic anemia with hemoglobin 63 g/L and hematocrit (PCV) 19.9%, normal MCV, low-normal MCHC, and platelets 304 x 10^9/L. Normal thyroid function, coagulation profile, blood glucose, and blood/urine tandem mass spectrometry (amino acid and acylcarnitine profiles). Negative hepatitis A, B, and C, syphilis, HIV, TORCH panel, EBV-IgM, and EBV DNA; positive serum cytomegalovirus (CMV) IgM. Stool microscopy showed 70-80 fat globules/HPF, and fecal pancreatic elastase-1 was severely reduced at 0.6 ug/g (normal >200 ug/g). Chest X-ray and echocardiogram were normal; abdominal Doppler ultrasound showed hepatosplenomegaly with normal gallbladder, biliary tree, and pancreas (parents declined cholangiography and liver biopsy).
objective.advanced_workup: Trio genetic testing identified compound heterozygous pathogenic variants in the CFTR gene in the infant: a paternal point mutation c.223C>T in exon 3 and a maternal heterozygous deletion of exons 2-3.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive genetic and biochemical diagnosis of cystic fibrosis (CF) presenting in infancy with cholestatic acholic stools, severe pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, steatorrhea, severe anemia, and hypoalbuminemic edema (confirmed by compound heterozygous CFTR mutations [paternal exon 3 c.223C>T and maternal exon 2-3 deletion] and fecal pancreatic elastase-1 of 0.6 ug/g, with incidental positive CMV IgM and exclusion of biliary atresia on ultrasound). Initial management with lactose-free medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) formula, oral ursodeoxycholic acid (30 mg/kg/day), and fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K failed to normalize stool color until oral Aspergillus oryzae pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy (1/2 tablet TID) was added, which restored yellow stools and promoted catch-up weight gain within 2 weeks.
